description:
Curious Mind in Disguise is tackling Planet X and SPHEREx with pure tech—no fluff. We’re building a web app that turns NASA infrared sky data into time-lapses and uses AI/Computer Vision to automatically spot moving objects and filter sensor noise.
AI/ML is covered! We need frontend/full-stack devs and astronomy/data geeks ready to ship real code. Join us!
summary:
We developed the SPHEREx Deep Space Telemetry Console, an interactive web dashboard that transforms multi-dimensional FITS data cubes into a zero-latency spatial and temporal analysis engine.

To address the challenge of rendering massive astronomical files in standard web browsers, we engineered a decoupled Python preprocessing pipeline. This pipeline astrometrically aligns raw SPHEREx data, suppresses background noise, and generates optimized Deep Median Stacks. Using OpenCV sub-pixel centroiding and mathematical Difference Image Analysis (DIA), the React frontend bypasses standard serverless timeouts by streaming lightweight, pre-processed temporal frames and spectral arrays from a Supabase edge network.

This project is important because it democratizes deep-space telemetry. By removing the computational bottleneck from the user interface, it empowers researchers and educators to instantly visualize stellar evolution, track moving transients, and analyze 102-band Spectral Energy Distributions directly in the browser, eliminating the need for complex local coding environments.
details:
Project Overview: SPHEREx Deep Space Telemetry Console

What does it do and how does it work?

Answer:The SPHEREx Deep Space Telemetry Console is an interactive, web-based analysis engine designed to process and visualize multi-dimensional astronomical FITS data cubes. It works through a decoupled architecture that separates heavy astronomical computation from the user interface. A custom Python data pipeline ingests raw NASA SPHEREx PT simulated data, astrometrically aligns the epochs using astropy.wcs and reproject, and mathematically flattens the temporal frames into a Deep Median Stack (Master Map). OpenCV (cv2.findContours) is then applied to extract exact sub-pixel centroids of celestial targets. Finally, an 11x11 bounding box extracts the peak flux into 102-band JSON arrays. This pre-processed telemetry and lightweight temporal imagery are pushed to a Supabase edge network, allowing the React frontend to query and render the data instantly without performing heavy client-side processing.

What benefits does it have?

Answer:The primary benefit is the elimination of the computational bottleneck typically associated with deep-space data. Researchers no longer need to download massive, multi-gigabyte FITS files or configure local Python environments just to inspect a region of the sky. The console provides zero-latency temporal scrubbing, allowing users to smoothly play back 60-epoch timelapses to observe stellar evolution. Additionally, its built-in Difference Image Analysis (DIA) engine instantly highlights transient moving targets—such as asteroids or novae—by mathematically subtracting static background stars, bringing critical anomalies to the forefront immediately.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Answer:The project aims to democratize deep-space astrophysics. By translating complex astrometric data into a highly visual, zero-latency browser interface, the console lowers the barrier to entry for analyzing NASA's SPHEREx mission data. It empowers citizen scientists, educators, and researchers operating on standard consumer hardware to actively participate in identifying transient celestial events, tracking Near-Earth Objects, and analyzing Spectral Energy Distributions without requiring enterprise-grade computing power.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Data Pipeline & Analytics: Python, Astropy (WCS alignment and reprojection), OpenCV (contouring and geometric image moments), and NumPy (percentile normalization and array sanitization).
  • Database & Cloud Storage: Supabase (PostgreSQL edge network for JSONB arrays and storage buckets for temporal PNG frames).
  • Frontend Framework: React (Vite workflow) deployed via Vercel, utilizing Tailwind CSS for responsive glassmorphism UI structuring.
  • Visualization: Three.js for rendering the interactive 3D Earth and satellite orbital mechanics, and Chart.js for graphing the 102-band spectral energy distributions.

How is your project creative?

Answer:The project creatively bridges the gap between strict scientific methodology and modern web engineering. Instead of relying on basic CSS blending to show differences between frames, we engineered a custom Mathematical Difference Engine in the browser. The frontend extracts raw HTML5 ImageData pixel arrays and dynamically calculates absolute intensity deltas using the formula |Frame A - Frame B| * 4.0 (Gain). This artificially brightens moving targets while suppressing the noise of static stars directly in the DOM. Furthermore, we integrated a cinematic 3D Three.js orbital visualizer alongside the raw data telemetry, merging high-level scientific utility with an engaging, immersive user experience.

What factors did your team consider? Our engineering decisions were heavily driven by the strict limitations of web browsers and serverless cloud architectures:

  • Serverless Timeouts: We initially considered querying the NASA IRSA Archive via SIA2 cutouts directly on the fly. However, we recognized that standard cloud functions (like Vercel) have a hard 10-60 second execution limit, which would result in 504 Gateway Timeouts when downloading and processing FITS cubes. This factored into our decision to build the decoupled asynchronous Python pipeline.
  • Browser Memory Exhaustion: Loading hundreds of raw temporal frames simultaneously crashes browser tabs (RAM exhaustion). We factored this in by mathematically subsampling massive stacks (like R Draconis) down to 60 evenly spaced epochs, preserving the temporal integrity while protecting client hardware.
  • Data Sparsity & Compliance: We had to account for fragmented spectral arrays from the D2/D5 detectors and extraction anomalies that produced floating-point NaN values at WCS boundaries. We implemented secondary Python sanitization loops to scrub these values, ensuring strict JSON compliance before database insertion.
